leading_positions.synthesis: Four members prefer B001 as the single prize part. All four name the same laureates (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) and cite nominal rigidities, staggered price and wage setting, policy rules and a microfounded policy framework. They share three points: the three names map onto separable roles (pricing device, contracts and rule, integrated normative framework); the ideas are 25 to 45 years old; and no recent prize covers this core. They do not share a view of the post-2008 and post-2021 empirical record. Strömberg and Friberg treat it as a limit on the claim, Strömberg stressing that the award rests on originating ideas rather than DSGE forecasting. Krusell reads it as a framework that was extended, not discarded. All four accept that the trio omits Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, who have real claims. Seven other members list B001 only as an alternative, which is not support for it as their preferred part. Strömberg moved from B015 first in the opening to B001 in round 1.

Three members prefer B006 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley. They share the view that the work made government an endogenous actor and joined formal theory to testable predictions. They also share the view that the attribution is comparatively clean, and that the roughly 25 to 30 years since the core work is ample time. All three name B001 as an alternative, and attribution is their stated reason for ranking B006 above it. All three concede that cross-country identification of constitutional effects is weaker than the theory. They also accept that the 2024 institutions prize is a real consideration, though each argues the discovery is distinct. They differ from the shortlist's opening pairing (Persson and Tabellini only) in keeping Besley as a separable state-capacity strand. Andersson, Krusell and Strömberg list B006 as an alternative only.

Two members prefer B002 with Kiyotaki and Moore. They share the view that the collateral-constraint mechanism is foundational and tractable, and that the two-author credit is unusually clean. They also share three reservations: the model is highly stylised, direct empirical identification comes mostly from later work by others, and the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises is a possible overlap. Dreber is more cautious about empirical support and doubts the entry can reach six votes. Both list B001 as an alternative. Fredriksson and Teorell list B002 as an alternative only. Andersson's opening ranked it eighth and Krusell's fifth, citing the 2022 overlap and the competing Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator strand. The chair is one of the two supporters, which is disclosed.

Two members prefer B021 with Helpman and Melitz. They share the view that firm heterogeneity and selection moved trade analysis from industries to firms, that it has been tested on firm-level data for over twenty years, and that the two-name attribution is among the cleanest. Redding is treated as a successor, a view Andersson also holds. Both agree the citation should centre on the selection model and not claim all firm-level trade research. Both flag credit for Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are off the entry, and sensitivity of welfare results to Pareto assumptions. They differ in emphasis on B001: Boppart lists B001 and B027 as alternatives and Fredriksson lists B001 and B002. Andersson, Dreber, Friberg and Krusell list B021 as an alternative only.

areas_of_agreement: Each of the four leading candidates is described by its own advocates and by members preferring other parts as a serious scientific contribution. Disagreement is mainly about attribution, identification and recent-prize overlap, not about whether a contribution exists.

Within B001, Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is the most defensible three-name cut among members who engage with attribution. Boppart's opening proposal used Galí in place of Calvo, and Boppart now calls Calvo-Taylor-Woodford the more defensible trio. Even B001's critics, such as Dreber and Enflo, describe the problem as attribution and not merit.
Kiyotaki and Moore is described by supporters, critics and non-supporters alike as the cleanest two-person attribution in macro.

Several members say support counts and elapsed time are not evidence of merit. Enflo and Teorell reject 'overdue' as a rationale, Stromberg and Fredriksson separate convergence of proposals from merit, and Dreber says shared first-place rankings should not count as merit.

Members agree the cross-country evidence on constitutional effects in B006 is weaker than the theory. Even its supporters say the citation should rest on the framework and testable predictions rather than on settled causal effects.
On the member files alone, B001 is the only entry that all eleven members either prefer (four) or list as an alternative (seven). This is not a vote count and implies nothing about hidden support.
scientific_disputes: B001: how the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation record bears on the framework. Krusell reads it as extended, not overturned. Strömberg and Dreber read the evidence as mixed or unresolved. Friberg notes that micro evidence on price adjustment shows state dependence the Calvo device does not capture. Members differ on whether this limits the claim or touches only the descendants of the originating ideas.

B001: whether the Taylor rule is a scientific contribution or a policy prescription (raised by Andersson), and whether the discovery is the originating ideas or the estimated, quantitative DSGE framework that made them usable.

B002: the model is stylised and its empirical importance is disputed. Supporters and critics agree that identification of the collateral channel comes mostly from calibrated or later work by others. They differ on whether that is acceptable for a foundational-mechanism prize.
B006: weight given to contested cross-country identification relative to the conceptual and empirical framework.

B021: whether quantitative trade models have superseded or only built on the heterogeneous-firm structure (Krusell versus Boppart), and how sensitive the welfare conclusions are to Pareto and other functional-form assumptions.

Cross-cutting: whether adjacent earlier prizes leave a distinct discovery. These are the 2022 prize (B002), the 2024 institutions prize (B006), Krugman 2008 (B021) and earlier macro prizes (B001). Members treat these as neighbouring or overlapping to differing degrees.
attribution_disputes: B001: eight names are credited. A Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio leaves out Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose claims concern the canonical New Keynesian model, identified estimation and central-bank adoption. Andersson also notes priority questions involving Fischer and Phelps, and Clarida is not on the ballot. Gertler also appears in B002, which complicates how a macro slot would be allocated.

B001 record-keeping: member statements describe convergence with differing counts (Dreber says eight of eleven, Friberg eleven of eleven). The shortlist's opening proposals show ten of eleven containing Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, because Boppart's opening used Galí in place of Calvo. This is a record difference, not a merit argument.

B002: Kiyotaki and Moore are proposed by all seven members who proposed a B002 laureate set. Gertler and Gilchrist (Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator) are credited on the ballot but not proposed. Adding them would change the laureate set or break the three-person limit.

B006: laureate sets differ between two and three names. The shortlist's opening proposals from Boppart and the chair named Persson and Tabellini only. Enflo, Hjalmarsson and Teorell argue Besley's state-capacity and political-agency work is a separable strand. The citation framing (constitutions and electoral rules versus also state capacity) bears on whether Besley is included.

B021: Helpman and Melitz leave out Bernard and Jensen (empirical firm-level facts) and Eaton and Kortum (parallel quantitative route), who are not on the entry. Fredriksson and Boppart would word the citation around the selection model rather than all firm-level trade research. Redding is treated as a successor by Andersson, Boppart and Fredriksson.

Other shortlist entries: B015 (Bresnahan versus Levinsohn) and B014 (Saez-Slemrod versus Chetty in different members' proposals) have unresolved attribution questions, but no member prefers them as a single part.
maturity_disputes: B006: whether the 2024 institutions prize makes a neighbouring award too soon. Krusell and Enflo call the topics neighbours rather than substitutes. Andersson, Fredriksson and the chair treat it as a brake or a timing concern. No member claims the core work is too young.

B002: the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize is seen by some as partly covering the theme and by others as a distinct mechanism, so the unclaimed ground is disputed. The collateral-constraint idea has had nearly three decades, but its empirical support comes largely from later work.

B001: the core ideas are 25 to 45 years old and tested through 2008, the zero lower bound and the post-2021 inflation. No member says timing is an obstacle. Members disagree about whether the post-2021 episode is resolved enough to treat the framework as settled.

B021: whether the firm-heterogeneity line is a distinct step from the new trade theory recognised in 2008 or a continuation of the same lineage (Krusell, Fredriksson and Friberg raise this, Boppart rejects it).
Several members distinguish maturity from merit. Krusell's description of B006 as 'arguably overdue' was challenged by Enflo and Teorell as not evidence of merit.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Chair: John Hassler prefers B002 and lists B001 and B014 as alternatives. Disclosed ties, none with a candidate, are co-authorship with committee colleagues Krusell, Boppart and Friberg (including the menu-costs paper with Friberg and Ellingsen, adjacent to B001 price-setting topics) and IIES affiliation with Krusell and Boppart.

Friberg: co-authored with the chair on menu costs and asymmetric price adjustment, which is adjacent to B001. His field proximity to B015 and B021 is also disclosed. He lists no co-authorship with credited candidates and says a public family relationship has no bearing on the candidates.

Boppart: long-running co-authorship with Peter Klenow (B050, not in his preferred configuration). IIES colleague of Torsten Persson (B006), frequent co-author of Krusell and the chair, and field proximity to B021 through his firm-dynamics research.

Krusell: field proximity to heterogeneous-agent macro as a successor literature to B001, and long-standing co-authorship with the chair and Boppart. Other members (Enflo, Hjalmarsson, Teorell, Fredriksson, Boppart) refer to a disclosed IIES proximity to Persson in his opening statement. His round-1 conflict note does not repeat it, so it is flagged here as reported by others.

Teorell: field proximity to B006 (comparative democratisation, quality of government). He lists co-authored work on corruption with an unspecified 'Persson' and states no claim that this is Torsten Persson. This is unresolved in the files and is not adjudicated.
Enflo: adjacent to political economy through work with Johannes Lindvall, and a Lund colleague of Andersson. Neither concerns the candidates.
Fredriksson: overlapped institutionally with the Stockholm/IIES environment from 2010 to 2017, with no recorded co-authorship with B006 candidates. His field is close to B010 and B047.

Dreber: research topically adjacent to B004, which she does not prefer. Hjalmarsson: field proximity to B010 and B047, which are not in her preferred part. Strömberg: adjunct at Chicago Booth and a long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell and others. Andersson: no connection to the B001 laureates is recorded.

These are disclosures, not adjudicated, and no recusal is assumed. Two cross-cutting points matter for B006: Persson's IIES links to several members, and the chair, Krusell and Boppart are frequent co-authors, none of whom is a candidate.
questions_for_round2: For B001 supporters and those listing B001 as an alternative: if the citation must name three, what specific criterion separates Calvo, Taylor and Woodford from Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets? Is it origin of ideas, identified estimation, or policy adoption? Would a different criterion change the laureate set or only the citation wording?

For B001: what evidence from the post-2021 inflation, state-dependent pricing and heterogeneous-agent critiques would distinguish a limit on the framework from a reason to doubt a prize centred on the originating ideas? Does the Taylor rule belong in the scientific citation or only in the practice record?

For B002: beyond calibrated models, which later empirical work supports the collateral-feedback amplification claim? Does the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises weigh against this mechanism more or less than the earlier macro prizes weigh against B001?

For B006: should the citation be framed around constitutions and electoral rules (Persson and Tabellini) or also around state capacity and accountability (adding Besley)? What concretely distinguishes the within-polity rules-to-policy programme from the 2024 institutions prize, and does that distinction survive if the identification evidence is judged weak?
For B021: does omitting Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum make a Helpman-Melitz citation incomplete, or can a selection-model citation stand? What separates it from the line recognised in 2008?

For all members: does your listed alternative represent a configuration you would support if your preferred part does not advance? If so, please state which laureate set and citation you would accept, so round 2 can distinguish alternatives from preferences. Which single piece of evidence or clarification would move you between B001, B006, B002 and B021?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows four distinct single-part preferences (B001 with four members, B006 with three, B002 and B021 with two each). No explicit preference reaches six, and the files do not support inferring more. B001 is the one entry every member either prefers or lists as an alternative, but members who do not prefer it mainly cite crowded attribution and a contested post-2021 record. Where members disagree, they mostly disagree about attribution boundaries, identification quality and overlap with recent prizes. The shared reference points for round 2 are Calvo-Taylor-Woodford, Kiyotaki-Moore, Persson-Tabellini with or without Besley, and Helpman-Melitz. The chair's own B002 preference and the disclosed co-authorship links are recorded, not adjudicated.
